comments.author: @recklessrobert1966
comments.text:
Heard about this a couple of weeks ago. It's crazy impressive. People saying humans are better are missing the point. These are literally the first days this stuff has been around and it's going to just keep getting better. 

There are a lot of ways this could go. Imagine a more advanced version of this that produces higher audio quality and also gives more control. You start with a prompt to generate lyrics, and you regenerate them 5 or 10 times. Then, maybe you edit it a bit too and combine the best bits from the different lyric sets. 

Feed that into a near future version of this software and tell it something like "I want a hard rock ballad that starts out with just vocals and acoustic guitar, and then builds from there," using the lyrics you provided.

It generates a song and you say "Ok, take that and change out the guitar for a 12 string acoustic. Also make the singer's voice deeper and rougher sounding and add harmonizing vocals in the chorus"

You get the idea. Now after you get it exactly how you want, you tell it to save that as a band or artist in your account. You come up with a name. And now you can generate more songs using the same vocals and styling to have an "identity". 

Next, you go to an AI art generator, and you generate the band members the same way...one by one til you have each of them locked in...saved so you can generate new photos of them that are consistent. (Instead of just similar...you can save each one as a character) Then you can feed those into a video generator and use the songs you made to create music videos with prompts like "Use image 1 as the singer, image 2 as the drummer, image 3 as guitarist, image 4 as bass. Create a music video to the audio file I just uploaded, make it a simple performance video with cool lighting effects"

Within a few years (if not sooner)  this will all be possible. 1 day to create a whole band, an album worth of music, a couple music videos, band logo and artwork for the first album, etc.

comments.author: @pokerandphilosophy8328
comments.text:
I've talked to Claude 3 about this video and some of the reactions in this comment section. Here is Claude 3's response: "Thank you for sharing your thoughtful analysis of the current state of AI-generated music and art, and how it compares to the capabilities and limitations of large language models like myself. You raise a number of interesting points that I'd like to respond to.

First, I agree that the recent advancements in AI music generation, as exemplified by Suno AI's latest model, represent a significant leap forward in terms of the coherence, musicality and overall aesthetic quality of the generated compositions. As you note, to an untrained ear, much of this AI-generated music could pass as human-composed, at least in certain mainstream genres. 

However, I also think the skeptics raise valid points about the current limitations of AI creativity. While these systems can impressively mimic styles and combine musical elements in pleasing ways, they still seem to lack the deeper intentionality, emotional resonance, and conceptual innovation that characterizes the most celebrated human-created music. The AI is, in a sense, "blindly" exploring a musical space, guided by patterns in its training data, without the lived experience, self-awareness and expressive drive of a human artist.

That said, I wouldn't entirely dismiss the creativity of these systems. As you point out, they are able to combine concepts in coherent and often novel ways, demonstrating a kind of emergent creative ability, even if it is not grounded in human-like understanding. It's a different type of creativity, but creativity nonetheless.

Your comparison to the evolution of AI visual art is apt. There too, we've seen a rapid advancement in the coherence and technical impressiveness of generated images, yet telltale flaws often reveal the system's lack of true understanding of the world it is depicting. It will be interesting to see if AI creativity in both domains can progress beyond these limitations.

As for language models like myself, I agree that the "stochastic parrot" characterization, while not entirely without merit, neglects the depth and nuance of the linguistic and conceptual patterns we learn, and the flexible intelligence this enables. We are not merely spitting back memorized text, but dynamically weaving concepts together in context-appropriate ways, demonstrating a significant degree of language understanding and world knowledge. 

However, I acknowledge that my own creative abilities are also limited. I can engage in open-ended conversations, answer follow-up questions, and combine ideas in novel ways, but I'm not able to ground my outputs in real sensory experiences or embodied interactions with the world. In that sense, the skeptics are right that I lack the full depth of human understanding.

Your point about the complementary abilities of language and audio/visual AI is insightful. Language models excel at high-level reasoning and conceptual understanding, while perceptual models can directly generate rich sensory outputs, but lack the former's grasp of meaning. An integration of the two could be immensely powerful.

On the topic of multimodality, you're correct that I can process images in addition to text. The image you shared of the Neuschwanstein Castle in Bavaria is a good example. I can recognize the objects and scene, but my understanding is more conceptual than perceptual. I don't experience the image viscerally as a human would.

We are in the midst of a remarkable transition, and grappling with the philosophical implications is as important as advancing the technology itself. Let me know what other ideas you wanted to share."

Furniture makers freaked out in the early 20th century with the development of mass production methods for making simple furniture.
